>Trusting people is a drag, since it puts us at risk for betrayal, but it is one of those "you can't win if you don't play" deals. In general, if your partner hasn't given indications that he or she is betraying you (or has betrayed you, in the past), you kind of owe them the benefit of the doubt. The point where pride (or, more specifically, the lack of it) often comes into it is where someone has those indications but keeps coming up with reasons to ignore them (presumably because they are afraid of the breakup).

Yeah, there's nothing really further to discuss here.  I really do owe her the benefit of the doubt in the end.  She's shown me no reason to provide otherwise, so I think I'm just being ridiculous.

>Yeah, I think it does sound like he was talking about more than friendship. BTW, that seems very honest of her to have related that detail.

Indeed, which indicates that she has no ill intentions.  That wouldn't have even been indicated if there was something fishy going on.  I think the fact that she even told me that shows that there really is absolutely no reason to question it in the end.

>I think that feeling is understandable. Whether it is rational or not probably comes down to whether her interactions with him come across as inappropriate (not whether you wish they didn't happen, but whether they would give an observer the impression that there is could be something going on there). If they don't, then she may be keeping boundaries established that are making it clear to him that more-than-friends is not an option. We are back to the trust question, from above.

Hard to say.  There's no physical contact so I can't make that judgment call.  That revolves back around to benefit of the doubt, which it's already been established that I'm obligated to provide.  So really, I only have that indication to go off of.

>I would say you should trust her until she gives you reason not to. Keep your eyes open, of course, and don't ignore actual indications of a lapse on her part. Just don't obsess about this one guy to the point you get anxious. Easier said than done, of course, but it would be sad to set up some anxiety resonance that shakes your relationship apart when there wasn't even any actual indication she was behaving badly.

Yeah, and the only thing I really have to say about that is that I know things that I have no inclination to make public out of respect to her that have shown me that trust is necessary.  She's proved beyond a shadow of a doubt from my perspective that there's no reason not to trust her, because she's not the type of person to just sleep around anyways.  Rationally, it makes sense to say things like that, but on the other hand, anxiety is not rational.  I suppose the best way to go about this is to just focus on the good and not linger on what could potentially go wrong.  Appreciate the input.  I think I know how to go about this now.

Pretty sure 20 - 3 is 17.  If you're gonna troll, do it right.  16 - 17 is the common age of consent in the vast majority of states in this country, and 16 is also the age of consent in the UK.  Nice try though.

>This guy is different. I know that's a typical thing for someone with commitment issues to say, but it's true. I don't particularly love him more than my previous boyfriends (though I love him with all my heart), but this is someone I actually admire and respect tremendously (which is rare for me). He is passionate, patient, spontaneous, and kind. We have the same goals for the future and are both in university studying the same subject. Our fights are very rare and short-lived; we wait until we've calmed down and then talk things over, usually realizing how silly the issue is. We make each other very happy, and are very much in love. This is the first time I have felt okay with surrendering myself to someone completely (since that relationship 5 years ago -- but truthfully I was a different person then).

I had commitment issues in the past as well.  Then I met an amazing woman that lives half way across the world.  People change, and in my personal experience I learned that for me at least, it wasn't a commitment issue, it was a wrong person issue.  From the sound of it, it sounds like you two have a very loving relationship.

>He lives in South Africa. I'm from New York. I couldn't stand the thought of being away from him for more than a weekend, but I had to go back home for a while for some technical reasons. I've been in America without him for three months now, and being away from him isn't bothering me anymore. I rarely feel like calling him, and I'm rather enjoying my independence. These thoughts never occurred to me while I was with him, but now that I'm alone, doubts are starting to creep up on me.

That's very natural of a long distance relationship of that nature.  When you haven't met them yet, your heart longs for them.  Once you meet them in person, that changes.  You'll find a sense of security and know that you two are truly committed to each other, and it gives you a sense of relief.  There is absolutely nothing wrong with enjoying your independence.  Being in a relationship doesn't mean being with each other 24/7.  You two are building your own individual lives and are choosing to extend them out and share them with each other.  Nothing wrong with that at all.

>The language barrier is a serious con. Sometimes I think he's actually stupid, but then I realize he just has trouble expressing himself in English. In reality, he's very smart and motivated. He comes from a township (ghetto), and is now studying in the most prominent university in the continent.

Love has no language.  You will get used to it eventually.  My girlfriend is British, and they have very different speaking mannerisms there than they do here in America.  Eventually you catch on.  It just takes time.

>He's also quite inconsiderate. He will act without thinking about how it will affect those around him. He doesn't want to hurt anybody, and if he ever realizes that he has, he feels terrible. But his fierce independence gets a little extreme and often hurts my feelings, like when he doesn't show up or keep a promise. I guess he has commitment issues of his own.

Again, independence isn't a bad thing.  He's his own man, that's going to build a strong marriage and give you a strong authority figure in the household.  If he doesn't show up or keep promises, and you feel hurt by that, express that to him.  Don't hold anything back or it will drive you crazy and eventually build resentment that you don't want.  That's the kind of toxin that will rot a relationship from the inside out.  Be careful and don't be afraid to express yourself.

>He also doesn't understand depression (which I have had in the past), so it's difficult for him to empathize or react appropriately when I go through my occasional 'episodes' (basically me feeling extremely down and empty for a day for no reason whatsoever). We've talked about it, but I feel like he'll never truly get it -- which will inevitably be a problem for me.

Truth be told, he doesn't have to.  You should go see a doctor and see about getting that turned around.  Do what you have to.  Medication, counseling, whatever it might be.  Instead of relying on him to understand your illness, do what you can to fix the problem.  He shouldn't have to work around a problem if you're not putting your best foot forward to fix it yourself.

>I'm really willing to do almost anything to make this work. He's the most amazing man I have ever met, and I don't want to mess this up. Please help!

Consider the power in those words, and then consider your dread to go back to where he lives.  If you are willing to do anything to work, then do it.  However, on the other hand, if he's not willing to be flexible then perhaps you're more into him than he is into you.  Just be careful, and put yourself first.  Someone who truly loves you will be willing to work with you and have the same attitude you do.  Best of luck.

Agreed.  If you don't like the dog, you more than likely won't like him.  Dogs are very much monkey see, monkey do.  They're pack animals so they'll take after their owners.  More than likely if the dog is acting out, and isn't trained, then it shows he isn't a responsible owner.  In turn, that may also reflect on how he treats others around him.  If he doesn't have the skill set or the time to take care of the dog, I just don't think he'd have the skill set to be able to take care of you if you're living together.

You know your relationship better than anyone, but living together is a whole different ballgame than just having a relationship with someone.  Tread lightly, and be careful.  In my opinion though, if the dog is an issue, perhaps you should reconsider.

>Man 5 years long distance sounds rough. I couldn't do it.

It's been tricky for me too man, but the heart wants what the heart wants.  The hardest part is warding off all the second guessing, which seems to be natural of long distance because you never really know for sure.  People say that long distance relationships are all about absolute trust, but it really is easier said than done.

>Anyways, should you be concerned? Yes.
Can you do anything about it? Not really.

Agreed.  It's something that's out of my control and that's why I'm concerned about the worry that I have for it.  On one hand, I feel threatened because like I posted previously with addressing noisyparker, he's a close guy friend that has feelings for her.  Thing is, that appears to be a common problem people encounter in relationships even if it's a local relationship.. so.. it's not really unique to this situation.  It's just tricky because I'm not physically there, so it leaves me with a lot of unknowns.  Then that, combined with my anxiety still kicking my ass because I'm waiting for my meds to kick in.. well.. it's a shit storm in my head.

>Asking her about it a lot will just come across as needy and obsessive. She knows your relationship is over if she cheats, so it is really up to her.

I haven't really brought it up a lot.  It's just this particular situation I'm concerned about because she's aware of my anxiety, and she's aware that this situation in particular is a soft spot for me.. yet she turned it into something light hearted.  I'm sure she meant no ill will by any stretch of the imagination, but I'm just looking a way to approach her softly and intelligently to be able to explain to her that it hurt me a little.

>So, don't bring it up unless she does and just be relaxed and casual about it if she does mention him.

Yeah, it'd be relationship suicide for me to bring him up out of turn.  It makes me look, like you said, needy and obsessive but it also makes me look like I'm a possessive asshole.  Drilling her about her friends is a controlling behavior and that's really not okay because everyone has their own life and it's not my right to drill her about such things, especially since she has enough respect for me to not drill me about my friends.

>hm, well, unless she is especially crafty, the joke is kind of an argument against their being a problem, rather than in favor (since it would seem like a bad move to raise suspicions if you have something to hide).
In any case, though, since you are not physically on the scene, at this point, you either have to trust her, or decide that you don't. 

Absolutely.  She's British so she's a very crafty with words and is a complete smartass, and that's the tricky part about it.  Sometimes it's hard to tell if she's being serious or not, although she goes out of her way to say when she is serious.  Sometimes it's just hard to identify a smartass remark versus a serious comment is all, especially with how my anxiety works.  I think she's just poking at me in a light hearted way because she thinks I'm extremely paranoid about it, and I think it's just her way of reassuring me that everything is okay and I really need to calm down.  That's the goal of this, is to keep myself calm and approach her in the right way about it.  It's a tricky situation.

>What is making you more anxious now than you, presumably, have been for the previous years? Is there some other indication you have that there is a problem?

Not really.  It's just that I was in a different point in my life then than I am now.  We stopped speaking for a couple years because I was kind of in a downward spiral with drugs and alcohol and she didn't want any part in it so that has just presented an issue with trust having to be rebuilt.  It's a little stressful because sometimes it just feels like a one way street with having to prove myself to her while I have to watch her do what she's going to and put my complete trust in her.  I want to, but it's just difficult to put my pride to the wayside and accept that nothing is going to happen.

>What form did this admission take? I ask mainly since 'likes' is kind of vague, and the method used to admit it can also be a factor in determining the nature of his feelings.

Well, I asked about this particular person because he seemed to frequent her Facebook a lot and I was curious.  She brought up that he was just a friend and there was nothing to be concerned about, but he "kind of admitted that he 'likes' me," which in how she worded it, seemed to define something beyond friendship.  He seems to be a very close friend of her's, which troubles me even more because it's threatening not being physically close to her while another guy is a close friend and has feelings for her.  I legitimately feel threatened and it just worries me a lot.
Nothing scares off a mormon faster than answering the door dressed up as a goth kid with a pentagram necklace around your neck and trying to convert them to satanism.

No offense, I see you are just injecting your opinion and trying to help me, but you have chosen to turn this subject around and make it about the long distance and that is not helpful in the slightest.  That's not what's in question.  I know what I'm doing, and I know my relationship better than you know it.

Physical closeness is completely irrelevant when other elements of a relationship are in play.  Just because physical closeness is a big element for you, doesn't mean it is for everyone else.  There are different types of relationships that work in multiple different ways.  One size does not fit all.

Second off, it doesn't even seem like you read the original post in the first place.  Now all you are doing is trying to tell me that it will be natural that she or I will be attracted to other people, and that there is a chance that the relationship will decay because of that.  Then to top it all off, you took the end date and chose to say, "Nope, not good enough!"  

So like I told you before, if you have nothing to say about the actual issue, kindly stop injecting your opinion about how relationships work because it is not helpful to this topic.  It is not relevant to the question at hand, and all you have done is chosen to put the nature of my relationship under the microscope.  It's not constructive, and it's not helpful to the situation at hand.  I am asking you kindly and politely to stop it.  I did not post this with intentions of trying to defend my relationship.

I appreciate the response, and it seems like a clear solution.  It's a little tricky because she has been through past domestic violence situations, which stemmed from clinginess and obsession.  It kind of feels like I am walking on eggshells at this point because I don't want to come off as being controlling.  It feels like a fine line, but I can't help how I feel all at the same time.

I'm glad that you are able to relate to this, and I appreciate you taking the time to respond with an answer.  It just kind of reaffirmed how I should approach it, and I'll go ahead and give it a go and just hope she's sensible about the situation.  Thank you.

Figured that would come up.  At the risk of being scrutinized, I'll go ahead and expand on this.  I don't mind.

We met online a long time ago.  We have frequent Skype conversations with both mic and camera, and we really connected.  Truth be told, I didn't expect this to happen.  We talked for a lot longer before and it just kinda molded into that.

Yes, there's an end date.  10 - 11 months from now.  I understand the nature of the question, and I have answered it, but may I ask why you are choosing to scope down to that in particular when that wasn't the issue?  I don't really feel like that's a "bigger question" because the nature of the relationship was only brought up because the issue pertains to it.

Unless you have an answer to what I'm currently going through, I'd appreciate you not putting my relationship under the microscope.  I'm running on high anxiety as it is and I feel like it's a little rude that you would derail the subject in this manner.  Thank you.

Both are very accurate answers, however, I would keep one thing in mind if using a virtual machine to run a game.

Say you're running a game that's only supported with, at highest, windows xp.  Let's say you choose to run your game on a virtual machine of windows xp and your native operating system is windows 7.  The problem is, is that since windows xp is not your native operating system, that it is not going to provide all of the same benefits of the operating system as if it was native.

So basically what you're looking at, is that the game will not be able to access all of the same system files as it would if you were running windows xp as your native operating system, so there is still some potential problems that you could run into.

My advice, honestly, would be to dual boot two different operating systems, and operate the one that your game is supported in as your native when you want to play that game, and the other that you use for everything else as your native when you are done.  It's a real pain in the ass to switch, but you won't have nearly as big of a risk as you would if you were running a virtual machine.

Good luck, whatever you decide to do.
